catalog_quote: [Stress] In Sereer, stress is assigned to the left-most long vowel of a word. When no long vowels are present, stress is assigned to the left-most stem syllable. Some noun tokens marked for stress: a.ˈtee.re 'book' o.ˈgef 'crack' xa.ˈkef 'cracks' o.ˈpaa.faañ 'clam digger' o.ˈpaa.fañ 'refuser' ˈmaa.lo 'rice' ˈdoo.le 'strength' dok.ˈtoor 'doctor' ˈqoox.ke 'bulls' 'gi.di 'gun' o.ˈtee.fan.ke 'cow walker' Some verb tokens marked for stress: a.ˈfoo.la 'jump' a.ˈsu.ma 'be hot' a.ɓo.ˈgoo.xa 'wash (refl.)' fa.ˈdii.di 'come in (imperative)' gee.ˈnoo.xaam 'I stand in place' aˌbaaj.baaj.'loo.xaa 'he's pretending to sing' [Phonological Inventory, Suprasegmentals] Stress is assigned metrically in Sereer. Stress is assigned to the left-most long vowel in a word; if there are no long vowels, then stress is assigned to the first stem syllable. Thus, stress is often realized on the penultimate syllable of a word. Due to these stress-assignment rules, many word-initial V syllables are not stressed. Coda consonants are extra-moraic, and thus do not seem to attract stress assignment. It is unclear at this point what the phonological correlates of stress are in Sereer. However, pitch or intensity or a combination of both can serve as a cue for a stressed syllable. [Kihm 2023 p.1] Comme le peul et le wolof, le sérère n'est pas une langue tonale. Un accent tonique frappe la première syllabe comportant une voyelle longue (cf. maalo /ˈmaːlo/ 'riz' vs. doktoor /dokˈtoːr/ 'docteur') ou, à défaut, la première syllabe du radical (gidi /ˈgidi/ 'fusil').

new_statements.translation: (Kihm 2023:) Like Fula and Wolof, Serer is not a tone language. A stress accent falls on the first syllable containing a long vowel (maalo 'rice' vs. doktoor 'doctor') or, failing that, on the first syllable of the root (gidi 'gun').

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files opened under (the target record's 'held' list is empty but the directory exists with 70+ files and a). (1) Internet Archive copy of linguistics.berkeley.edu/sereer/guestwiki 'Stress', 'last edited on 30 April 2013, at 18:37'): the page text reads exactly 'In Sereer, stress is assigned to the left-most long vowel of a word. When no long vowels are present, stress is assigned to the left-most stem syllable.' followed by 11 noun tokens (a.ˈtee.re 'book', o.ˈgef 'crack', xa.ˈkef 'cracks', o.ˈpaa.faañ, o.ˈpaa.fañ, ˈmaa.lo 'rice', ˈdoo.le, dok.ˈtoor 'doctor', ˈqoox.ke, 'gi.di 'gun', o.ˈtee.fan.ke) and 6 verb tokens (a.ˈfoo.la, a.ˈsu.ma, a.ɓo.ˈgoo.xa, fa.ˈdii.di, gee.ˈnoo.xaam, aˌbaaj.baaj.'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress goes to the leftmost syllable with a long vowel; if the word has no long vowel, stress falls on the first syllable of the stem (noun-class prefixes such as o-, a- are skipped, so prefixed words surface with second-syllable/penultimate stress); coda consonants do not count for weight. Not a tone language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No rule given; one token is transcribed with a secondary mark on a reduplicated pre-stem element (aˌbaaj.baaj.ˈloo.xaa 'he's pretending to sing'); Heath 2014 notes both copies of a doubled verb are stressed, the second more heavily.
new_statements.exceptions: The wiki's own token gee.ˈnoo.xaam 'I stand in place' has stress on the second long vowel rather than the leftmost; Redeye's 2012 handout tokens oˈtʃige:n 'sister' and ˈomaag 'river' also do not follow long-vowel attraction, and she notes 'plural marker attracts stress' (aˈlas 'tail' ~ ˈχalas 'tails', i.e. the singular a- prefix is unstressed). Loanword dokˈtoor shows final stress via the long vowel. Acoustic correlates said to be unclear (pitch and/or intensity).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated over the (prefix+)stem word; class prefixes excluded from the default ('left-most stem syllable'). Tokens are citation forms elicited in a field-methods class from one Saalum-dialect speaker. Phrase level: 'Phrase-level stress in Sereer is on the final stressed syllable' (Heath 2014: 215).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement comes from the UC Berkeley 2012-13 field-methods wiki, which explicitly describes the Saalum (Saloum) dialect [saal1237] (consultant Malick Loum), not Seereer-Siin [sine1238], the standard/best-described variety (McLaughlin 1992-2005, Fal 1980). Kihm's 2023 fiche is titled 'seereer siin' but its accent rule and examples (maalo, doktoor, gidi) are taken from the Berkeley Saalum wiki, its sole bibliographic reference. Renaudier 2012 describes the Mar Lodj variety (Niominka area, niom1238) and is silent on accent. No dialect differences in stress are reported anywhere I read.
